Leveraging on innovative computational techniques, the SYSMAGRAD project investigates the coupling between supramolecular materials of various nature and concentration gradients. Biomaterials naturally couple with the chemical gradients that surround them, giving rise to properties such as autonomous motion, self-catalysis, and regeneration. item.title: Incarico di ricerca: Photoluminescence, Raman, and near-field spectroscopic studies on III-V nanowires (ROMA "La Sapienza")
item.description:
Deadline: 2026-12-19 23:59
Institution: ROMA "La Sapienza", Roma
Field: Physics / 02/PHYS-03 Fisica sperimentale della materia e applicazioni

As part of the ERC StG NANOWHYR project (grant number: 101042349), we will investigate the photoluminescence and Raman signal generated by III-V nanowires (GaAsN, InN, InAsP, etc.) involved in the ERC project in a near-field mode, integrated with different substrates. We will assemble a near-field microscope and connect it to a new photoluminescence setup and both pulsed and continuous lasers. We will also investigate the possibility to use the near-field tip to locally anneal hydrogen in hydrogenated III-V nanowires, to form localized emitters.

The research will investigate interface instabilities and quantum transport between two coupled Bose–Einstein condensates in relative motion and characterized by distinct order-parameter structures. Finite-temperature effects will be described through a self-consistent kinetic many-body framework that couples the dynamical evolution of the condensates to a quantum kinetic equation for the thermal components, including mean-field interactions, collisions, and particle exchange between the condensate and thermal cloud. This approach will enable the study of how the normal component modifies instability onset, transport, dissipation, and vortex nucleation beyond conventional zero-temperature…

Field: Physics / 02/PHYS-04 Fisica teorica della materia, modelli, metodi matematici e applicazioni

Innovations and novelties concern, at a fundamental level, human activities, social behaviours, and biological systems. The vast majority of these systems are intrinsically open systems: new, previously unknown elements may continuously emerge. Statistical and dynamical regularities are shared by systems featuring innovation, pointing to general, i.e., non-system-specific, mechanisms underlying the innovation process. We will deepen the study of a class of Pólya-urn-based models that reproduce many of the empirical behaviours observed in real-world systems, while searching for novel relevant observables to characterise the latter.
